You've written about about 250 words explaining why people (men in particular) should not want to get divorced in the USA, but your argument against marriage boils down to "marriage often leads to divorce, and nobody should want to get divorced in the USA." What does this miss? (Besides, as Siimo mentioned, the fact that divorce is not as common as you think and that rate is tilted by a relatively small group of people with a large number of failed marriages.) Well, it misses even the most obvious benefits associated with marriage:

  • Religious approval
  • Family approval
  • Tax breaks
  • Power of attorney
  • Inheritance
  • Spousal coverage (e.g. medical)

Despite the nastiness associated with divorce, those who are still married are in the religious, social and legal sense a privileged class. Assuming your own beliefs don't outright require that you get married, those of your family might (particularly older relatives), and even now much of American society looks down on families that choose not to marry. Moreover, the government significantly rewards those who do get married: income-splitting (significant for families with a homemaker or disparate incomes), mandating spousal benefits, differences in the inheritance process and so on are substantial financial incentives. Moreover, in the case of LGBT individuals (those most prominently fighting to get married), the inequities of heterosexual divorce really aren't a factor: divorce can be nasty, but the big problem right now is that the playing field is so tilted you could set up a slalom course. LGBT couples are less likely to have mutual children (i.e. adopted, IVF or similar rather than children from a prior relationship), more likely to have similar income and assets, and more likely to be treated equally by the legal system if (or when) they do divorce.

To some degree, you're right in saying that heterosexual men should not want to get married in the USA. For them (depending on the exact circumstances), the benefits associated with marriage are very often outweighed by even the chance of suffering a high-conflict divorce. Your mistake is in assuming that the risks which apply to that one class are equally present and applicable to all others - the risk isn't worth it for men, but women are on the other side of the playing field and LGBT people on a different playing field altogether. As a result, it's hard to say that "nobody" should want to get married: at most, it can be said that marriage is often a poor proposition for certain classes of people.

My parents have been married for over 40 years. I have been married for over 10. Marriage is hard work - and sometimes people are lazy. That does not mean that no one should want it.

Should marriage rates be lower than they are? Sure - if people were less delusional about what love is, and realize that they themselves are not mature enough for the commitment they are making... marriage rates should go down. However, that does not mean those people who do understand what marriage really means should be denied that.

My relationship with my wife was "functionally" identical before we were married compared to after. We owned a house together, had no children. Marriage did not change that for us. But it did change my commitment to her. It did make us fight harder for ourselves and each other.

And it did one more very important thing. In the eyes of the law a marriage is legally close to a business partnership. What this means is that I can handle "business" for my wife - and she can handle "business" for me - making it easy for us to divide and conquer tasks that society will not allow to be divided between a boyfriend and a girlfriend.

In the end, marriage is difficult, and hard, and yet rewarding in ways that being just a SO cannot be. You could never pay for your girlfriend's college education (you'll never get anything if she dumps you) but you can pay for your wife's - because if she does get a great job because of that education you'll be right there knowing she is with you for the long haul.
